latin.390: Humana etiam testimonia, cum de religione, & voluntate Dei agitur, haud satis tuta videntur. Si injustae, quis ausus fuit eas esse non indignas Deo dicere? De sententiis Judicum anne justae, an injustae, meum non est judicare; Dei hae sunt partes, cui illi rationem judiciorum suorum sunt reddituri. Coguntur nonnulli a supremis Magistratibus conservandae Reipublicae causa nonnulla facere, quibus minime delectantur, sed quid hoc facit ad id de quo inter nos agitur? Sive justae sunt, sive injustae eiusmodi sententiae, annon tutius est de Dei voluntate & sententiis ex Scriptura judicare, perfecta fidei nostrae regula, & plena voluntatis Dei erga nos revelatione, quam ex humano aliquo exemplo?
latin.391: GAR. Imo si forte sentiret aliquis, haec ita fieri non debere ab hominibus, sed iis judiciorum suorum normam esse debere legem illam Judaeis datam de filiis pro crimine patris non puniendis, Deut. 24. 16. tamen haudquaquam inde consequeretur, Deum etiam in suis judiciis ab eadem norma non posse discedere; cum ipse nullis legibus obstringatur, sed sua sit ipsi voluntas agendorum norma & lex.
latin.392: PLAC. De potestate Dei hic non quaeritur, sed de eius justitia, quam partim datis legibus, partim sanctissimis sententiis, quibus eam a calumniis Judaeorum vindicavit, qualis sit patefecit. Quid est, cur his eius revelationibus non acquiescamus potius, quam hominum judiciis, aut opinionibus? Unde enim potius cognoscatur legislatoris justitia, & quid probet, quam ab eius lege? Nullis quidem legibus obstringitur Deus, nempe alterius; at suis ipsius legibus quid est quare se se ultro obstringere non possit? Sua ipsi voluntas est agendorum norma & lex; non certe praecise quatenus est voluntas, sed quatenus est optima, justissima, sanctissima voluntas, eademque sapientissima, itaque nihil insipienter, nihil injuste, nihil male velle, aut facere potest. Necessario enim volitio congruit cum voluntatis universali perfectione. Determinatur igitur voluntas Dei ad bene volendum a sua ipsius justitia &c.: non potest enim suae ipsius perfectioni, hoc est, sibi ipsa repugnare.
latin.393: GAR. Sed quod secundo adjungimus, nobis legem illam adversus perduelles in hoc negotio proponentibus non ea mens est, ut putemus cogitationes nostras de Dei justitia ad legum humanarum normam exigendas esse. Nulla hactenus animum subiit cogitatio eiusmodi. Sed quia, qui peccati primi imputationem negant, hac inter alias ratione utuntur, quod religio nostra Judaeis & Ethnicis huius dogmatis assertione in odium adducatur, tanquam injustum aliquid crudele divinitati attribuens, nos hoc exemplo docemus, illis injustum aut barbarum videri non posse, quod ipsimet in suis publicis judiciis tam frequenter observant. Non ergo ita colligimus: Homines perduellium liberis peccata paterna imputant. Ergo & Deus censendus est peccatum Adae posteris imputare. Sed ita potius: Hominibus sive Ethnicis, sive aliis non videtur injustum, si in crimine laesae-Majestatis filius pro peccato patris poenas ferat. Quis igitur ex illis poterit Deum injustitiae arguere, si peccatum Adae puniat in posteris? Ut exemplum non ad confirmandam veritatem usurpetur, sed ad illustrandam tantum, & ab injustitia aut immanitatis accusatione vindicandam.
latin.394: PLAC. Si haec eius mens fuit quicum mihi res erat, aequum fuisset, ut eam innueret apertius: non enim sum Oedipus. Quicquid sit, praeter ea quae hactenus a me sunt observata, quominus ad id accommodatum sit hoc exemplum duo vel tria obstant, illud primo, quod in eo exemplo non agitur nisi de poena temporali, cum imputari dicatur peccatum Adae ad mortem aeternam, nec ad eam tantum, sed etiam ad poenam quae sit peccatum, & hominem in eo statu constituat, ut non possit deinceps non peccare. Hoc enim est quod potissimum repugnare judicis & legis justitiae nobis videtur. Deinde, si quidam ex hominibus criminis paterni imputationem liberis aut nepotibus approbaverunt, non defuerunt ex altera parte, & fortasse multo plures qui improbaverunt: Commemorat nonnullos ipse vir doctus pag. 81. 82. 83. potuisset multo plures si voluisset. Itaque non medetur scandalo similitudo nisi forte ex aliqua parte. Praeterea, quid simile afferri potest eiusmodi imputationi, quae etiamnum post aliquot annorum millia grassatur in omnes posteros, nemine quidem excepto? Denique eiusmodi exempla vel ira extorsit, vel necessitas tuendae vitae principum & salutis reipublicae: quorum neutrum in re de qua agitur locum habet. Imo tantum abest ut imputatione illa immediata peccati Adami homines a peccando inhibeantur, ut contra priventur bene agendi seu obediendi habitu, & subijciantur necessitati peccandi: id quod a fine legis & justitiae vindicis vehementer abhorrere videtur.
latin.395: GAR. … contendimus, [legem] quae omnibus hominibus lata est, in qua testatur Deus se vindicare peccata patrum in filios Exod. 20. 5. [non] ad particulare factum, quod Deus Judaeis singulariter praescripsit, Deut. 24. 16. aut ad particularem oeconomiam, qua se in causa Judaeorum usurum significat Ezech. 18. 20. Sed de his locis fusius postea dicendum erit. PLAC. Miror legem Deut. 24. 16. vocari a viro docto particulare factum, & oraculum, quo justitiam suam Deus vindicat a calumniis Judaeorum, Ezech. 18. particularem oeconomiam; nec minus miror iis duabus legibus opponi legem Exod. 20. 5. quasi haec causae nostrae obesset. Nam & lex illa erat universalis regula omnium judiciorum, in quibus de crimine aliquo agebatur, & particularis oeconomia non potuisset, nisi respectu cuiusdam temporis, justitiam Dei vindicare ab objecta injustitia, & lex Exod. 20. si quam imputationem innuit, innuit tantum mediatam seu consequentem, cum declaratione divinae justitiae Ezech. 18. minime pugnantem. Proinde melius Augustinus (verba sunt Zanchii exponentis secundum Decalogi praeceptum) Tom. 8. in Psal. 108. qui locum hunc Exodi interpretatur de illis impiorum filiis, qui parentum impietatem imitantur: ac proinde poenam etiam aeternam illis hoc loco denunciari docet, propter iniquitatem, quae ita parentum fuit, ut etiam facta sit propter imitationem filiorum. Atque inde hoc probat, quod addit Deus, eorum qui oderunt me: odium enim hoc refert tum ad patres tum ad liberos. Ita nihil pugnare locum Exodi cum loco Ezechielis ubi Dominus pronunciat, filium nempe simpliciter innocentem non portaturum iniquitatem patris, nimirum neque aeternam neque temporalem. Exod. enim 20. sermonem esse de liberis non simpliciter innocentibus, sed qui patrum iniquitatem imitentur. In his verbis habemus conjunctam duplicem autoritatem Augustini & Zanchii: Habes supra pag. 132. etiam Hieronymi; quibus consentiunt alii omnes, aut saltem prope omnes interpretes, ut mirum sit potuisse hanc Dei legem pro imputatione immediata a quoquam afferri.

pass_a.390: Placeus: human testimonies are not safe enough when religion and God's will are at stake. If the sentences are unjust, who dared call them worthy of God? Judging whether they are just belongs to God, to whom judges answer. Compulsion by supreme magistrates for the republic does not settle our dispute. Just or unjust, it is safer to read God's will and sentences from Scripture—faith's perfect rule and God's full revelation—than from a human example. Tip after truncated magistrate tip.
pass_a.391: GAR: even if someone thinks men ought to take Deut. 24:16 (sons not punished for the father's crime) as the norm of their judgments, it still does not follow that God cannot depart from that same norm in his own judgments, since he is bound by no laws and his will is his own norm and law of what is to be done.
pass_a.392: Placeus: the question is not God's power but his justice, shown in given laws and in holy sentences vindicating him from Jewish calumnies. Better to rest in those revelations than in human opinions. A legislator's justice is known from his law. Bound by no another's laws, he may still bind himself by his own. His will is norm and law not bare as will but as best, just, holy, and wise—so he cannot will or do foolishly, unjustly, or badly. Volition matches the will's universal perfection; God's will is determined to willing well by his own justice and cannot contradict itself.
pass_a.393: GAR's second point: proposing the law against traitors does not mean measuring God's justice by human laws. Deniers say asserting first-sin imputation makes religion hated among Jews and Gentiles as cruel to God; the example shows what they themselves practice in public judgments cannot seem unjust to them. Not: men impute traitors' sins to children, therefore God imputes Adam's sin. Rather: Gentiles do not think it unjust if in lese-majesty a son suffers for the father—so who of them can charge God with injustice if he punishes Adam's sin in posterity? The example illustrates and vindicates; it does not prove.
pass_a.394: Placeus: if that was his opponent's mind, he should have said so plainly—Placeus is no Oedipus. The example fails (1) because it concerns only temporal penalty, while Adam's sin is imputed to eternal death and to a penalty that is itself sin and necessitates further sin—the main clash with a judge's and the law's justice; (2) many on the other side disapprove father-to-child or grandson imputation as well as approve it (pp. 81–83 and more if he wished); (3) nothing like an imputation ranging even now after millennia over all posterity without exception; (4) such examples come from wrath or necessity of guarding princes' lives and the republic's safety—neither applies in the matter at hand. Immediate imputation of Adam's sin does not curb sinning but strips the habit of doing well or obeying and subjects men to necessity of sinning, against the end of the law and of vindicating justice.
pass_a.395: GAR contends the law for all men in which God testifies he vindicates fathers' sins on sons (Exod. 20:5) is not to be reduced to the particular act God singularly prescribed to the Jews (Deut. 24:16) or to the particular economy of Ezek. 18:20—more on these places later. Placeus marvels that Deut. 24:16 is called a particular act and Ezek. 18 a particular economy, and that Exod. 20:5 is opposed to them as if it hurt the cause. Deut. 24:16 was a universal rule of all criminal judgments; a particular economy could still vindicate God's justice for a time; Exod. 20 if it hints any imputation hints only mediate or consequent, in no way clashing with Ezek. 18's declaration of divine justice. Better: Augustine via Zanchi on Ps. 108 reads this Exodus of sons of the ungodly who imitate parents' impiety—hence even eternal penalty—and "who hate me" refers to fathers and children alike; so Exodus and Ezekiel agree that a simply innocent son bears neither eternal nor temporal iniquity of the father. Jerome (p. 132) and nearly all interpreters concur; strange anyone could bring this law for immediate imputation. Tip before second similitude (Thomas / human body).

390: Even human testimonies, when religion and God's will are in view, do not seem safe enough. If those sentences are unjust, who dared to say they are not unworthy of God? Whether judges' sentences are just or unjust is not mine to decide; those parts belong to God, to whom they will render account of their judgments. Some are compelled by supreme Magistrates, for the republic's preservation, to do things in which they take no delight—but what does that make for the matter between us? Whether such sentences are just or unjust, is it not safer to judge of God's will and sentences from Scripture—the perfect rule of our faith, and the full revelation of God's will toward us—than from some human example?
391: GAR. Indeed, if someone should happen to think these things ought not so to be done by men, but that the norm of their judgments ought to be that law given to the Jews about sons not being punished for the father's crime, Deut. 24:16—still it would by no means follow from that that God also cannot depart from the same norm in his judgments; since he is bound by no laws, but his own will is to him the norm and law of what is to be done.
392: PLAC. It is not God's power that is asked here, but his justice, which he has disclosed partly by the laws he gave, partly by the most holy sentences by which he vindicated it from the Jews' calumnies. Why should we not rather acquiesce in these revelations of his than in men's judgments or opinions? Whence is a legislator's justice, and what he approves, better known than from his law? God is indeed bound by no laws—namely of another; but by his own laws, why may he not freely bind himself? His own will is the norm and law of what is to be done—not precisely as it is will, but as it is the best, most just, most holy will, and the same most wise; and so he can will or do nothing foolishly, nothing unjustly, nothing badly. For volition necessarily agrees with the will's universal perfection. Therefore God's will is determined to willing well by his own justice, &c.: for it cannot contradict its own perfection—that is, itself.
393: GAR. But as to what we add second: when we propose that law against traitors in this business, our mind is not that our thoughts of God's justice are to be measured by the norm of human laws. No such thought has yet entered our mind. But because those who deny the imputation of the first sin use this among other reasons—that our religion is brought into hatred with Jews and Gentiles by asserting this dogma, as attributing something unjust and cruel to the divinity—we teach by this example that what they themselves so often observe in their public judgments cannot seem unjust or barbarous to them. We do not therefore gather thus: Men impute fathers' sins to traitors' children. Therefore God also is to be thought to impute Adam's sin to posterity. But rather thus: To men, whether Gentiles or others, it does not seem unjust if in the crime of lese-majesty a son bears penalties for the father's sin. Who then among them can charge God with injustice if he punishes Adam's sin in posterity?—so that the example is used not to confirm the truth, but only to illustrate it and to vindicate it from the charge of injustice or monstrosity.
394: PLAC. If that was the mind of him with whom I had to do, it would have been fair that he hint it more openly: for I am no Oedipus. Be that as it may, besides what I have so far noted, two or three things stand in the way of this example's being fitted to that end. First: in that example only a temporal penalty is in view, whereas Adam's sin is said to be imputed unto eternal death—and not to that alone, but also to a penalty that is itself sin, and sets a man in a state where he cannot thereafter not sin. That is what seems to us chiefly to clash with a judge's and the law's justice. Next: if some men have approved imputing a father's crime to children or grandsons, there have not been wanting on the other side—and perhaps far more—who disapproved. The learned man himself mentions some on pp. 81–83; he could have mentioned many more if he wished. So the likeness does not heal the scandal, except perhaps in some part. Further, what like thing can be brought for an imputation that even now, after some thousands of years, ranges over all posterity, none excepted? Finally, such examples either wrath extorted, or the necessity of guarding princes' lives and the republic's safety—neither of which has place in the matter at hand. Indeed, so far is that immediate imputation of Adam's sin from keeping men from sinning that, on the contrary, they are stripped of the habit of doing well or obeying, and subjected to a necessity of sinning—which seems violently to abhor from the end of the law and of vindicating justice.
395: GAR. … we contend that the law laid down for all men, in which God testifies he vindicates fathers' sins upon sons, Exod. 20:5, [is not to be reduced] to the particular act God singularly prescribed to the Jews, Deut. 24:16, or to the particular economy by which he signifies he will deal in the Jews' cause, Ezek. 18:20. But of these places more fully later. PLAC. I marvel that Deut. 24:16 is called by the learned man a particular act, and that the oracle by which God vindicates his justice from the Jews' calumnies, Ezek. 18, is called a particular economy; and I marvel no less that to those two laws Exod. 20:5 is opposed, as if it hurt our cause. For that law was a universal rule of all judgments in which some crime was treated, and a particular economy could not—except with respect to a certain time—vindicate God's justice from the injustice objected; and Exod. 20, if it hints any imputation, hints only a mediate or consequent one, in no way clashing with the declaration of divine justice in Ezek. 18. Better therefore Augustine (Zanchi's words, expounding the second commandment of the Decalogue), Tom. 8 on Ps. 108, who interprets this Exodus place of those sons of the ungodly who imitate their parents' impiety, and so teaches that even eternal penalty is denounced to them here for iniquity that was so the parents' that it also became the sons' by imitation. And he proves it from God's adding "of those who hate me": that hatred refers both to fathers and to children. So Exodus does not clash with Ezekiel, where the Lord pronounces that a son simply innocent will not bear the father's iniquity—neither eternal nor temporal. For Exod. 20 speaks of children not simply innocent, but who imitate their fathers' iniquity. In these words we have the joined double authority of Augustine and Zanchi; above at p. 132 you have Jerome too, with whom all—or at least nearly all—interpreters agree, so that it is strange anyone could bring this law of God for immediate imputation.
